own_scenes.desc: DJ Spanish Fly ganó en el Club No Name (1985-86) el concurso de DJs y el de rap, pinchó la radio y regaló miles de cintas de 808 atronadores; compraba a ciegas todo lo de Profile y así encontró «Drag Rap» de los Showboys, con la sintonía de Dragnet: el ritmo Triggerman, base del Gangsta Walk o Buck Jump, un baile en círculo, tribal, el primero que los duros podían bailar. El sello On the Strength de Reginald Boyland lanzó a Gangsta Pat («I’m Tha Gangsta»), Al Kapone («Lyrical Drive-By») y a 8Ball & MJG, que le pusieron nombre y que en Houston, con Suave House de Tony Draper, grabaron Comin’ Out Hard (1993) y el «pimpin’» de «Space Age Pimpin’». La escena vivía de las mixtapes de DJ Squeeky, DJ Zirk y de DJ Paul y Juicy J, que con Three 6 Mafia (Mystic Stylez, 1995) fueron precursores del horrorcore y del crunk; los DJs cobraban y los raperos no. Del soul, el gospel y el blues de Sun y Stax venían sus samples, y de ese ritmo a tresillos, dicen, nació el trap.

notes.chapter: Cap. 18: The South Got Something to Say
notes.text: Hustle & Flow (2005) de Craig Brewer, financiada por John Singleton y con Terrence Howard como un chulo que quiere ser rapero, devolvió el foco a Memphis, eclipsada por el crunk de Atlanta: Three 6 Mafia fue el primer grupo de rap en ganar un Óscar con «It’s Hard Out Here for a Pimp» y «Whoop That Trick» de Al Kapone entró en el Hot 100. «Stay Fly» (Most Known Unknown, 2005) unió por fin a Three 6, 8Ball & MJG y Young Buck, de Nashville; después vinieron Yo Gotti, Young Dolph o Moneybagg Yo.

refs.q: Gangsta Walking was the first dance that was cool for hood dudes to do.
refs.para: Al Kapone (artist, Memphis): Gangsta Walking was the first dance that was cool for hood dudes to do. Because you wasn’t really fully dancing, you basically was just walking in a circle. It was a little tribal thing. But you could only do it to certain beats, like a Triggerman, which was the Showboys’ “Drag Rap.”

refs.q: If you wanna hear the raw shit, you gotta get the mixtapes.
refs.para: Al Kapone (artist, Memphis): If you wanna hear the raw shit, you gotta get the mixtapes.

refs.q: It was always that underlying beat that had that feel, no matter what style of music you put on it, and that beat is what we feel like is where trap originated from.
refs.para: One thing I can say about Memphis, the vibe of the beats always stayed the same, but you could hear old-school soulful songs sampled, which made those beats more pimpin’, and those are more of what 8Ball & MJG rapped off of. You would take that same drum pattern, put eerie and scary sounds on it, and that would get you that wicked vibe. You’d take the exact same drum pattern and just put chants on it to make people get crunk or get buck. It was always that underlying beat that had that feel, no matter what style of music you put on it, and that beat is what we feel like is where trap originated from.

Al Kapone (artist, Memphis): Hustle & Flow did wonders. Because at the time when that movie came out, Atlanta, they were the top dogs, because the whole Atlanta crunk thing had completely overshadowed Memphis. The Memphis hip-hop scene, we had got buried. By the time Hustle & Flow came out, it was like, finally, people were talking about Memphis again because of songs like “Whoop That Trick,” because of songs like “It’s Hard Out Here for a Pimp.” It put a spotlight back on us.
